modules.name: Networking
modules.broke: Two computers. No shared memory. The only way to know anything about another machine is to send a message and wait — and the message may never arrive. Every single thing in distributed systems is a consequence of that one fact.
modules.buys: A name resolves to an address (DNS). An address becomes a reliable ordered byte pipe (TCP). The pipe becomes private and authenticated (TLS). The tunnel carries a request and gets a response (HTTP). That is the whole internet, and you can now walk it end to end.
modules.costs: Reliability is bought with latency — that is head-of-line blocking, and it is why UDP exists, why HTTP/2 did not fix what it claimed to, and why QUIC was built. And the wire gives you one machine. The moment there are ten of them: where does the truth live? That question is a database.

atoms.trap: The internet is 4 layers. OSI's 7 are a teaching artifact you must be able to NAME but will rarely use.

modules.name: Foundations
modules.broke: Nothing yet — this is the floor. It was silently skipped, and that is a debt, not a choice. Every system you will ever design runs on one machine with a finite CPU, a memory hierarchy spanning six orders of magnitude, and a scheduler that can take the CPU away mid-sentence. You cannot reason about a distributed system until you can reason about one.
modules.buys: The ability to say why something is slow instead of that it is slow. Locks, races, deadlock, and the event loop — the machinery under every line of Node you have ever written.
modules.costs: Nothing breaks next. This module is the one that stops later modules from breaking. Skipping it is why isolation levels look like arbitrary SQL trivia instead of what they are — a concurrency problem in a SQL costume.

atoms.t: CPU and the memory hierarchy (register → L1/L2/L3 → RAM → SSD → disk → network)
atoms.trap: Jeff Dean's latency numbers are ~2010 — several are now wrong by 10×. Teach them as intuition; ESTIMATE with napkin-math.

modules.name: Databases
modules.broke: You have ten servers now, and they are disposable — any one can die mid-request and be replaced by a fresh one. So where does the truth live? It cannot live in a process's memory, because processes die. That question IS a database.
modules.buys: A single place that survives a crash and can be concurrently written by many clients without them corrupting each other. That second half is the entire hard part, and it is why this module is gated on Module 0.
modules.costs: The database is now the bottleneck — one box, and every request goes through it. It also gets slow the moment it is popular. The obvious fix is to keep a copy of the hot answers somewhere fast. That is a cache, and it instantly hands you a consistency problem — because now there are two copies of the truth.

atoms.t: Relational vs NoSQL (KV / document / column / graph)
ACID — what each letter actually promises
Isolation levels & serializability — DERIVE them, do not memorise them

atoms.trap: REQUIRES M0 atoms 0.5–0.7. This is a concurrency problem wearing a SQL costume. The ANSI phenomena are ill-defined — the paper proves it and defines snapshot isolation.

modules.name: Caching
modules.broke: The database is the bottleneck. Every request pays a disk seek for an answer that has not changed in an hour. The same question is being asked ten thousand times a second and answered from scratch every time.
modules.buys: Orders of magnitude. A RAM hit is ~100ns; a disk seek is ~100µs–10ms. That is the memory hierarchy from atom 0.1, cashed in.
modules.costs: Two copies of the truth. The instant you cache, you own an invalidation problem — and invalidation has no correct answer, only trade-offs. Then the cache itself fails in ways the DB never did: stampede, thundering herd, hot keys. And when you try to fix consistency across many caches on many machines, you find you need the machines to agree — which nobody has taught you how to do yet.

atoms.t: Why caches exist · the cache hierarchy
Redis internals — single-threaded event loop (the SAME epoll story as atom 0.10)

modules.name: Scalability
modules.broke: One box cannot take the load. Not the DB, not the app server, not the cache. You must add boxes — and every box you add is a new way for the system to be inconsistent, unbalanced, or on fire.
modules.buys: Boxes without chaos. Statelessness (so any box can serve any request), consistent hashing (so adding a box does not re-shuffle every key), rate limiting (so one client cannot take the system down), and the ability to estimate before you build.
modules.costs: Now failure is partial. Before, the system was up or down. Now three boxes are fine, one is slow, and — the killer — a slow machine is indistinguishable from a dead one. You cannot even tell what state your own system is in. That is the door into distributed systems, and it is the intellectual core of the whole program.

atoms.t: Stateless vs stateful — the property that makes horizontal scaling possible at all

atoms.ref: ties forward to atom 1.16 (L4 vs L7)

modules.name: Distributed Sys
modules.broke: The machines must now agree — and there is no global clock, messages are lost, and a slow machine is indistinguishable from a dead one. You cannot ask 'is node B alive?' You can only ask 'has B replied yet?', and 'not yet' is not an answer.
modules.buys: The intellectual core of the entire program. Ordering without a clock (Lamport, vector clocks). Agreement despite failure (quorum, Raft). A precise vocabulary for what a system actually promises (the consistency lattice) instead of a marketing page's word for it.
modules.costs: Coordination is expensive and it couples. Every consensus round is a round trip; every synchronous call means if B is down, A is down. The escape is to stop calling B and instead write to a log that B reads at its own pace — which is Messaging.

atoms.t: Failure detectors — why 'is it dead?' is undecidable
Physical clocks — and why you cannot trust them
Consistency models — linearizable → sequential → causal → eventual
atoms.trap: Jepsen also documents real databases VIOLATING their own claimed guarantees. Read the analyses, not the marketing page.

atoms.ref: Raft paper + raft.github.io viz + MIT 6.824 Raft lab

atoms.t: Distributed locks — and why they are a trap

modules.name: Messaging
modules.broke: Synchronous calls couple services. If B is down, A is down. If B is slow, A is slow. If B needs to be redeployed, A takes the outage. You have built a distributed monolith with extra network hops.
modules.buys: Put a log between them. A writes to the log and leaves; B reads at its own pace; B can be down for an hour and lose nothing. The log is durable, replayable, and ordered — and that ordering is what makes it a truth rather than a buffer.
modules.costs: Everything becomes eventually consistent, and 'exactly-once' turns out to be a lie — the network cannot tell a lost message from a lost acknowledgement, so the best you get is at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer. That is atom 1.10 coming back to collect. Also: ordering only holds per-partition, and now you need patterns for multi-service workflows — Saga, outbox, CQRS.

modules.name: Storage
modules.broke: The database holds rows you query. It does not hold a 4GB video, or ten years of clickstream, or a petabyte you want to scan analytically. Different access patterns need different storage, and forcing them all into Postgres is how you get a $40k/month bill.
modules.buys: Blob storage for the big opaque things. Erasure coding for durability at a fraction of replication's cost. Columnar layout for the scans (this is your ClickHouse work, explained).
modules.costs: Now the truth is scattered across several stores with different guarantees, and keeping them coherent is its own job.

atoms.t: ⭐ Columnar storage — ties directly to your ClickHouse work

modules.name: Observability
modules.broke: You have built something you cannot see. It is 3am. It is down. Something in a graph of forty services is slow and you do not know which. What do you look at?
modules.buys: The ability to answer that question in minutes instead of hours. Metrics tell you that. Traces tell you where. Logs tell you why. And SLOs tell you whether you are even allowed to care — an error budget is permission to fail.
modules.costs: Observability is not free — cardinality explodes, tracing adds overhead, and an alert that fires too often trains you to ignore it.

atoms.t: Logging — structured, and what NOT to log
Metrics — RED (rate, errors, duration) and USE
Alerting — SLI / SLO / SLA and error budgets

modules.name: Security
modules.broke: TLS gave you a private tunnel to a server whose identity you verified. It told you nothing about who the human on the other end is, or what they are allowed to do. Atom 1.9 solved the wire. It did not solve the user.
modules.buys: AuthN (who are you) held apart from AuthZ (what may you do) — the single most-confused pair in the industry. Plus the crypto vocabulary to reason about it instead of copying a Stack Overflow answer.
modules.costs: Every mechanism here is a new attack surface. A JWT you cannot revoke. A session store that is now a bottleneck. An OAuth flow with one redirect misconfigured.

atoms.t: AuthN vs AuthZ — identity vs permission
Sessions vs JWT — the revocation problem

atoms.ref: revisits atom 1.9 — this is the DH/cert distinction, generalised

atoms.t: Hashing & salting — why a password is never encrypted
TLS in depth — revisits atom 1.9 with the full picture
CSRF / XSS / SQLi / SSRF — at a DESIGN level, not a payload level

modules.name: Infrastructure
modules.broke: You have a design. It runs on your laptop. Now put forty copies of it on machines you have never touched, replace them one at a time without dropping a request, and make it reproducible by someone who has never met you.
modules.buys: Reproducibility and safe change. A container is a machine you can diff. Blue-green and canary make a deploy reversible — which is the only thing that makes deploying often safe rather than reckless.
modules.costs: An enormous amount of accidental complexity, and an orchestrator that is itself a distributed system with its own consensus (etcd → Raft → atom 5.10).

atoms.t: Docker — and what an image actually is
Containers vs VMs — the isolation boundary

modules.name: Advanced
modules.broke: A single business action now spans five services and five databases, and there is no transaction that can span them. 2PC exists and everybody avoids it. So how do you book a flight, charge a card, and reserve a seat — atomically — when 'atomically' is not available?
modules.buys: The patterns that make multi-service correctness possible without a distributed transaction: Saga, outbox, event sourcing, CQRS. These are what senior engineers actually reach for.
modules.costs: Enormous conceptual overhead, and every one of them is eventually consistent by construction. Reach for them when you must, never because they are impressive.

atoms.t: ⭐ The outbox pattern — the fix for 'write to DB AND publish' not being atomic

modules.name: High Level Design
modules.broke: You now know every mechanism. You still cannot design a system — because designing is not recalling mechanisms, it is choosing between them under constraints you had to extract yourself, and defending the choice when someone pushes.
modules.buys: A framework that survives an hour of pressure: requirements → estimation → API → data model → architecture → scale → reliability → tradeoffs. And fifteen real designs, each of which you must defend, not recite.
modules.costs: Nothing breaks after this — but it is also the module that will most tempt you to shortcut. Grokking is deliberately NOT on this list. It teaches the shape of an answer instead of the machinery, and it rewards exactly the discriminator-dodging reflex already logged as your blind spot.

atoms.t: The framework: requirements → estimation → API → data model → architecture → scale → reliability → tradeoffs
atoms.ref: built from Modules 1–10, not from a book

modules.name: Low Level Design
modules.broke: Inside every box on your HLD diagram is code — and a beautiful architecture made of unmaintainable classes is still unmaintainable. The unit of design is COMPLEXITY, not patterns.
modules.buys: Deep modules, information hiding, and the ability to name a refactoring move instead of gesturing at it. Refactoring 2e is smell → NAME → mechanics on every page — which is an unusually good fit for a term-decay blind spot.
modules.costs: Nothing — but note the traps: Clean Code is NOT on this list (it installs rules to obey rather than a model to reason with), and GoF's patterns half-collapse into plain functions in TypeScript. Applying them as classes in Node is cargo-cult.

atoms.t: Refactoring — design as named, safe, REVERSIBLE moves
SOLID — as heuristics to RE-DERIVE, never as commandments

atoms.trap: Half of GoF (Strategy, Command, Factory Method, Template Method, Iterator) collapses into plain functions and closures in TS. Consult GoF only for its Consequences sections — the costs, which every free site amputates.

atoms.ref: ⭐ Cosmic Python (derives it from the pain it solves)

modules.buys: The performance layer: clarifying requirements out loud, whiteboarding legibly, articulating a tradeoff as a tradeoff rather than a preference, and STAR stories that are true.

terms.etymology: the item at the **head** of the **line** (queue) **blocks** everything behind it
terms.concept: One lost packet freezes every READY packet behind it. TCP's cost is LATENCY. This is why UDP exists.
terms.note: Derived UDP FROM it in S4 — then could not name it in S5.

terms.etymology: a **retransmit** that is **fast** — it does not wait for a timer
terms.concept: Wire FLOWING → receiver re-ACKs the last in-order byte → 3 duplicate ACKs → resend immediately.
terms.note: 'I don't know what the other mechanism is' (S5) — then re-derived it from scratch minutes later.

terms.concept: Wire SILENT → no signal can exist → a TIMER expires → resend + exponential backoff.
terms.note: Described it perfectly; never said the name.

terms.concept: ACKs are cumulative — 'the next byte I expect is N.' Receiving 3,4,5 while 2 is missing re-sends 'expecting 2' each time.

terms.etymology: the wait grows **exponentially** — double it each failure
terms.concept: RTO fires → resend → DOUBLE the timer → resend → double again.

terms.etymology: the attacker is **literally standing in the middle**
terms.concept: Diffie–Hellman alone shares a secret with WHOEVER IS THERE, not with WHO THEY CLAIM TO BE.
terms.note: ⚠️ Called the CA 'the middle man'. The middle man is the ATTACKER. The CA is a trusted third party.

terms.concept: The trusted third party whose signature vouches for the server's identity. Pre-installed in your browser. CERT = IDENTITY. DH = SECRECY.

terms.etymology: named for its inventors — the ONE term here that really is arbitrary
terms.concept: The shared secret is BUILT INDEPENDENTLY ON BOTH ENDS and is NEVER SENT. The attacker sees both public halves and cannot un-mix them.

terms.etymology: the **anchor** on which all **trust** rests — fixed, shipped in advance
terms.concept: Hardcoded root DNS IPs ≅ pre-installed root CAs. You must trust SOMETHING in advance to escape the 'who do I trust first?' regress.

terms.etymology: *idem* (same) + *potens* (power) → **the same effect however many times applied**
terms.concept: N runs leave the same end STATE as one run. NOT the same response.
Client attaches a unique id; the SERVER records processed keys and returns the original result on retry. A POST tool — not a GET feature.

terms.etymology: **safe** to call — it cannot hurt anything
terms.concept: Changes NO server state at all. A pure read. GET. safe ⊂ idempotent ⊂ all.

terms.etymology: **multiplexing** = many streams into one wire · **de**-multiplexing = **splitting them back out**
terms.concept: The OS KERNEL reads the destination PORT and hands bytes to the listening process. Routers read the IP; the kernel reads the port.
terms.note: Historically fused: 'Nginx chooses the port.' It does not.

terms.etymology: it **resolves** the name, **recursively** walking the chain for you
terms.concept: The actor that DOES THE WALKING. Root/TLD/authoritative only POINT.

terms.etymology: it is the **authority** on this domain — the source of truth
terms.concept: The ONLY tier that holds the actual A record. root → TLD → authoritative.

terms.etymology: how long this record gets to **live** before it must be re-fetched
terms.concept: Bounds the cache. Past its TTL a record is STALE — not an error.

terms.etymology: old, not wrong-shaped — it **confidently points at the old address**
terms.concept: Loud failure = old server gone (timeout). QUIET failure = old server alive → you silently hit the wrong box. Quiet is more dangerous.

terms.etymology: it makes an **effort**, the **best** it can — and **promises nothing**
terms.concept: IP: packets may be lost, reordered, duplicated, corrupted, unacknowledged.
Purpose: SYNC STARTING SEQUENCE NUMBERS, BOTH DIRECTIONS. Liveness is a side effect. Two messages confirm only one direction.
